title: A Family Too Vast to Count
story:
Who could count the Yadavas? The book that tries to answer the question asks it in the middle of trying. It begins with a phrase about the man at the center of the count: Krishna, established in the highest duty of the householder, the one who keeps the home-fire.

Then it begins to count, and the counting fails almost immediately. Sixteen thousand and more than a hundred queens made their home in Dwaraka. Eight of them are named in an earlier passage as the chief among the jewel-women, Rukmini at their head; the rest pass through the account as a crowd. On every one of these queens Krishna begot ten sons. The arithmetic alone runs past a hundred and sixty thousand — more sons than any father could know by face, more than any court could hold.

Among so many, a few names rise to the surface: Pradyumna, who carried the war to Shalva's illusions and to Bana's city; Aniruddha, who had been stolen away and brought home again; Samba; Diptiman; Bhanu; Pushkara; Vedabahu; Shrutadeva; Sunandana. And behind the names, the text is at pains to say, stretched a line no one could number. No one born in this family was poor, and no one had few children; the men of the line of Yadu were famous for their deeds. Where the old reckoning attempts a total, it runs into the crores and beyond, and then the book simply stops and asks: who could count the Yadavas?

Through the middle of that river ran the course of the firstborn. Pradyumna married the daughter of Rukmi, and their son Aniruddha married Rukmi's granddaughter — the same house joined twice over, as if to bind the line with a double knot. From Aniruddha came Pratibahu, and from Pratibahu, Subahu, names that trail off into a line too long to follow. But one name from this line the text holds up like a seed: Vajra, the grandson of Pradyumna through Aniruddha, who alone would survive the destruction by the mace — the last days of Dwaraka, when the Yadava houses would turn their own weapons upon one another and leave the whole unnumbered family to a single thread.

And why such a family at all? The book offers a reason. In the great war between the gods and the demons, terrible demon-lords had been slain; to hold such forces in check, the text says, the gods themselves took birth in the line of Yadu. Hari — Krishna himself — stood among them as their measure and their master, the one against whom the whole line was weighed.

Having said all this, the book turns from counting to the smallest record: how Krishna slept, sat, walked, spoke, played and bathed among his family. After millions upon millions, the truest measure of the man turns out to be an ordinary day in the middle of it all — a householder at the home-fire, exactly where the passage began.
reflection: The passage counts what cannot be counted and then stops to ask who could — the unnumbered family becomes the sign of the divine's entanglement with human history, gods taking birth in Yadu's line to hold the demons in check. Against that ocean of names, the single survivor, Vajra, stands out as the whole continuity reduced to one thread.
next_story_tease: Before the counting, there was the beginning: Dwaraka's founding days, and Balarama's marriage to Revati.
hero_scene: In the great courtyard of Dwaraka, Krishna sits among his queens and sons — the gathered thousands of the Yadu house stretching out of sight, Rukmini at his side and children at his knees.
